title: PURA Final Decision — Docket 14-09-09: Utilities Billing of GRT and Use Tax
text:
STATE OF CONNECTICUT

PUBLIC UTILITIES REGULATORY AUTHORITY
TEN FRANKLIN SQUARE
NEW BRITAIN, CT 06051

Docket No. 14-09-0914-09-09
PURA Investigation of Utility Billing of Gross Receipts and Sales and Use TaxesPURA Investigation of Utility Billing of Gross Receipts and Sales and Use Taxes

August 3, 2016

By the following Commissioners:

Michael A. Caron
John W. Betkoski, III
Arthur H. House

Lead Staff: D. Gillich
Legal Advisor: R. Luysterborghs

DECISION

DECISION
INTRODUCTION
Background of the Proceeding
On September 10, 2014, pursuant to §§1619 and 16-19e of the General Statutes of Connecticut (Conn. Gen. Stat.), and on its own motion, the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (Authority) established the above-cited docket to review whether the utilities are correctly assessing the appropriate gross receipts tax (GRT) and sales and use taxes (SUT) on customers’ bills and associated issues.
Conduct of the Proceeding
By Notice of Request for Written Comments dated September 25, 2015, the Authority requested comments regarding the application of the GRT and the SUT on customers’ bills. By Notice of Hearing dated January 8, 2015, the Authority scheduled a public hearing on these matters on Friday, January 30, 2015, at its offices, Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, CT. The hearing was held as scheduled. Oral arguments were not requested and the Docket was closed on July 28, 2016.
Parties to the Proceeding
The Authority designated the following as Parties to this proceeding: The Connecticut Light and Power Company (CL&P) and Yankee Gas Services Company (Yankee) both d/b/a Eversource Energy, P.O. Box 270, Hartford, CT 06147-0270; The United Illuminating Company (UI), Connecticut Natural Gas Corporation (CNG), The Southern Connecticut Gas Company (Southern), P.O. Box 1564, New Haven, CT 06506-0901; Office of Consumer Counsel (OCC), Ten Franklin Square, New Britain, CT 06051; Commissioner of the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, 79 Elm Street, Hartford, CT 06106; Retail Energy Supply Association (RESA), 280 Trumbull Street, Hartford, CT 06103 and Cleary Energy, P.O. Box 6208, Wolcott, CT 06716.
Relevant statutes for grt assessment

Pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-264 and §12-265 the electric distribution companies (EDCs) and the local natural gas distribution companies (LDCs) are assessed a GRT by the Department of Revenue Services (DRS) based on their operating revenues before expenses.
Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-264 states:

(c) (1) Each electric distribution company, as defined in section 16-1, or municipality, or department or agency thereof, or district manufacturing, selling or distributing electricity to be used for light, heat or power, providing electric transmission services, as defined in said section 16-1, or electric distribution services, as defined in said section 16-1, shall pay a quarterly tax upon its gross earnings in each calendar quarter at the rate of (A) eight and one-half per cent of its gross earnings from providing electric transmission services or electric distribution services allocable to other than residential service and (B) six and eight-tenths per cent of such gross earnings from providing electric transmission services or electric distribution services allocable to residential service.
Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-265 states:

(b) (1) Each company and municipal utility included in section 12-264, other than an electric distribution company, as defined in section 16-1, included in subsection (c) of section 12-264, and other than a municipality, or department or agency thereof, or district manufacturing, selling or distributing electricity to be used for light, heat or power, shall be taxed at the rate of five per cent upon the amount of gross earnings in each taxable quarter from operations, except as set forth in subsection (c) or (d) of this section and except that each company and municipal utility manufacturing, selling or distributing gas or electricity to be used for light, heat or power shall be taxed at the rate of four per cent upon the amount of gross earnings in each taxable quarter allocable to residential service, but deduction shall be made of gross earnings (A) from all sales for resale of water, steam, gas and electricity to public service corporations and municipal utilities, whether or not such purchasers are Connecticut public service corporations or Connecticut municipal utilities, and whether or not they are subject to the tax imposed by this chapter, (B) from any federal BTU energy tax included in adjustment clause and base-rate revenues, (C) from sales of appliances using water, steam, gas or electricity by each such company of the net invoice price plus transportation costs of such appliances, (D) of electric and gas companies, as defined in section 16-1, from energy conservation loan programs, (E) from all sales for resale of gas to companies registered pursuant to section 16-258a, and (F) from all sales of natural gas to a user or entity located outside the state.
Positions of Parties
Pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. §§12-264 and 12-265, the EDCs and LDCs are assessed different statutory GRTs for residential and commercial operating revenues, although the actual rates differ.
Gross Receipts Tax
CL&P, UI, CNG, Southern and Yankee (Companies) explained that the GRT is assessed on utility operating revenues as opposed to individual utility customer bills. The GRT is applicable to distribution service charges (DIS) as well as a number of non-distribution tariff charges. The GRT is built into the DIS charges in two distinct ways. CL&P, UI, CNG and Southern include the same company-wide weighted-average GRT in their respective tariffs, while Yankee includes the true statutory GRT in its tariffs. Companies Responses to Interrogatory RA-1. The EDCs have built the GRT into such non-distribution tariff charges as:

Transmission (TRA);
Competitive Transmission Assessment (CTA);
System Benefit Charge (SBC);
Conservation (CON);
Conservation Adjustment Mechanism (CAM);
Renewable Energy (RE).
UI and CL&P/Yankee Responses to Interrogatory RA-7.
The LDCs include the GRT in the following tariff charges:
Purchased Gas Adjustment (PGA);
Conservation Adjustment Mechanism (CAM).

CNG and Southern Responses to Interrogatory RA-7.

Many of these charges are established in separate administrative proceedings. The application of the GRT depends on the nature of the charge to which it is applied. For example, an electric TRA charge includes a company-level, weighted-average GRT to avoid having separate TRA charges for residential and commercial customers. UI Response to Interrogatory RA-1. With regard to the PGA, since that charge is already differentiated by customer class, the LDCs include the appropriate customer class GRT in the PGA charge. CL&P/Yankee, CNG and Southern Responses to Interrogatory RA1.
The Authority has full discretion to build GRT recovery into rate class tariffs as it deems appropriate, even if that amount is different from the one assessed by the DRS. CL&P and Yankee Responses to Interrogatory RA-9; Tr. 1/30/15, pp. 21 and 22; CL&P/Yankee Brief pp. 3-5; UI Brief pp. 3-7.

Sales and Use Tax

The EDCs and LDCs collect the SUT from non-residential customers and remit it to the DRS. The SUT is a separate line item on the applicable customers’ utility bills. The EDCs calculate the tax by multiplying the current SUT rate of 6.35% by the total current monthly charges less an exemption of $150. For LDC customers, the SUT calculation is simply the current SUT rate of 6.35% multiplied by the total current monthly charges. There is no monetary exemption for LDC customers. The EDCs and LDCs are not aware of any problems with their respective processes for applying the SUT to customer bills. Therefore no adjustment to the process is needed. Companies Responses to Interrogatories RA-17 and RA-20.

RESA expressed concern related to the situations where electric supplier charges are included on the EDC bills, otherwise known as consolidated billing. In such situations, the EDC controls whether a customer will be taxed for the supplier charges. Using consolidated billing, the EDCs collect the SUT on behalf of the suppliers and remit those taxes to the state. However, suppliers are ultimately responsible for the accurate assessment and remittance of such taxes. RESA contended that the EDCs do not always assess the appropriate tax on customer bills. For instance, RESA members have encountered circumstances where customers who are taxable are not charged the sales tax. While in other instances, the EDCs have credited sales tax to customers as part of cancelled billing transactions even though they were not charged the sales tax on those bills. RESA Written Comments dated October 24, 2014, pp. 2 and 3.
RESA members also have experienced instances in which the EDCs have assessed different tax rates to the same account from one month to the next without any discernable basis. Compounding this problem, when the EDCs have incorrectly charged or failed to charge taxes on a bill that includes electric supplier charges, they have generally been unwilling to correct those errors with respect to the supplier charges. Instead, the EDCs have been requiring the suppliers to resolve the error outside of the respective EDC’s billing process. As a result, suppliers are required to either issue refunds or separate bills to customers to resolve the EDCs’ original errors. Customers who receive consolidated bills from the EDCs reflecting supplier charges are not accustomed to receiving separate bills from their suppliers; making it difficult and, in some cases, impossible for suppliers to collect on such bills. RESA was also concerned about the EDCs properly applying the sales tax exemption for the first $150 of a customer’s bill in any given month. Id., p. 3.
RESA requested that the EDCs be required to: (a) fully document the processes they use to assess, collect and remit sales taxes on behalf of electric suppliers and implement appropriate changes to those processes to ensure that any deficiencies are corrected; and (b) allow suppliers, through electronic data interchange (EDI) transactions, to designate whether a particular customer should be charged sales tax on the supplier services portion of the EDC bills. RESA Written Comments dated October 24, 2014, p. 3.
UI stated that RESA’s claims with regard to its assessment of the SUT are unsubstantiated. Further, it was not aware that RESA or any of its members had any issues with its assessment of the SUT. UI stated that it would discuss any issue with RESA directly. UI, CNG and Southern Brief, p. 14. CL&P and Yankee also argued that the assertions made by RESA were without merit and suggested that a separate technical meeting would be the appropriate forum to discuss fully the concerns of RESA. CL&P and Yankee Brief, p. 8.

Commercial Customers Providing Residential-Like Services

CL&P and Yankee consider those entities providing residential-like services such as nursing homes to be commercial customers and are billed at the general service rate. Pursuant to DRS Ruling 99-3, Yankee offers nursing homes the option to take service at a residential rate when such facts are similar to the facts in their ruling. Nursing homes must present such evidence to receive residential service. The GRT is reflected in the rate class under which the customer receives service. CL&P/Yankee Response to Interrogatory RA-4.

Based on their initial review, CNG and Southern indicated that nursing homes are taking service at commercial rates. There are various types of facilities for individuals such as hospitals that care for individuals on a transient basis while other facilities essentially become an individual's home. CNG and Southern suggest that where the facility lies on this spectrum could assist in determining whether the facility is residential or commercial and what GRT to assess. CNG and Southern Responses to Interrogatory RA-4.

Authority Analysis
The original GRT has evolved over time. Initially, all utility operating revenue was assessed a single GRT. The later introduction of a residential discount established the two-tier GRT that exists today where the residential GRT is lower than the non-residential GRT. The GRTs for the EDCs were increased during electric unbundling to compensate for the loss of GRT revenues previously received from utility generation. Legislation further carved out exceptions for specific types of businesses like marinas and agriculture. Simultaneously, the EDCs practiced tariff choice, which allowed customers to reduce their bills by electing to receive service under any tariff. Currently, a limited number of residential customers receive commercial service and vice versa as a direct result of legislative exceptions and tariff choice. The DRS assesses the GRT based on utility “Class of Service” (COS), which refers to residential and non-residential as opposed to tariff service. Consequently, the utility is assessed the residential GRT for residential establishments receiving commercial tariff service even though these customers pay a non-residential GRT to the utility.

Based on its investigation to assess whether the utilities are correctly assessing the appropriate GRT and SUT on customers’ bills, the Authority reviewed the following issues: 1) whether the gas and electric distribution companies are correctly recovering the appropriate GRT and SUT from customers; 2) whether a nursing home or similar facility qualifies as a residential or commercial customer for purposes of receiving service from gas and electric distribution companies and for collection of gas and electric companies gross revenue tax and sales use tax expenses; 3) whether the statutes governing public service company rate setting require that gas and electric distribution companies assess and recover their GRT and SUT expense from residential and commercial customers at the same rates that gas and electric distribution companies are taxed by the DRS and 4) associated issues.

Gross Receipts Tax
The Authority’s overarching goal of tariff design is to establish distribution rates such that each tariff class provides the utility with a fair and equitable return on rate base. Determining rate of return requires the apportionment of hundreds of expense and capital accounts into tariff-specific income statements and balance sheets. The GRT is only one expense of many dealt with during tariff construction. Presently, the GRT is built into Yankee tariffs using statutory rates while all other utilities use a weighted average rate applicable to all tariffs. Under the average GRT, residential customers pay more than the statutory rate while non-residential customers pay less. The average approach was introduced to maintain revenue neutrality as independent electric generators grew under electric unbundling. Tr. 1/30/15, p. 57. Nonetheless, Connecticut is beyond unbundling and the practice is inconsistent with the notion of equitable distribution rate design wherein tariffs reflect costs incurred by the utility to service the tariff class.

Currently, Yankee performs its cost allocation and stage one tariff development absent the GRT. Tariffs are then finalized by including the appropriate statutory GRT rate in each tariff. Under this approach customers pay the true statutory GRT built into their service tariffs. Since the vast majority of customers continue to utilize the tariff initially assigned by the utility, their GRT payment to the utility will match the utilities’ GRT assessment made by the DRS. A potential mismatch will exist when customers elect an alternative tariff to reduce their bills. Although the Authority understands that this mismatch could be addressed through duplicate tariffs that differ only by the GRT, the additional administrative burden on the utility, billing software expense and potential customer confusion preclude this approach. Similarly, modifying billing software to apply the statutory GRT based on individual customer COS would prove expensive and also require utilities to qualify individual customers. Since dual GRT-differentiated tariffs or the equivalent billing practices will not be ordered by the Authority, all customers, including those exercising choice, will be required to pay the GRT built into their service tariff. The choice for many EDC customers will come down to choosing between the residential tariff containing the statutory residential GRT and a small commercial tariff containing the statutory non-residential GRT. Going forward, the EDCs and LDCs will be directed by the Authority to develop distribution rates in a rate application to include the true statutory GRT as Yankee presently does.

Many non-distribution charges already reflect the statutory GRT rate distinction. Charges that currently use a weighted average GRT will be altered to reflect statutory rates. Since the new GRT treatment in tariffs will not take place until each utility’s next general rate increase application, the changes in non-distribution charges will be made following approval of new rates. The modest mismatch between GRT assessments and ratepayer payments that the Authority anticipates will be reviewed in each utility’s next general rate increase application.
Sales and Use Tax
Unlike the GRT, the SUT is imposed upon the individual customer. Pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. §12-408, the sale of all tangible personal property is subject to a SUT in Connecticut. However, certain utility customers are exempt from paying the SUT. Pursuant to Conn. Gen. Stat. §12412(c), utility customers classified as residential are exempt from paying the SUT. Customers coded as non-residential may qualify for the exemption by submitting to the utility a DRS CERT-115 form. Once the utility receives a properly executed form, the account is coded so that the SUT will not be charged. Companies Response to Interrogatory RA-19.
Since no RESA representative attended the hearing, the Authority inquired, on behalf of RESA, if each EDC offers an EDI service capability to retail suppliers. Both EDCs stated that they do and were willing to discuss any issue with RESA directly. Tr. 1/30/15, p. 101. UI stated that they were not aware of having being contacted by RESA. UI Brief, p. 14. Consequently, the Authority sees no reason to intervene at this time in the EDCs’ normal business relationships with RESA who should discuss their concerns with the EDCs directly.
Commercial Customers Providing Residential-Like Services
While all of the utilities consider such entities as nursing homes to be commercial in nature, the manner in which each utility assesses the GRT is not uniform. For example, Yankee provides residential tariff service to nursing homes that demonstrate that their care model reflects the types of situations discussed in DRS Ruling 99-3. CL&P/Yankee Response to Interrogatory RA-4. DRS Ruling 99-3 speaks to utility GRT assessment, as opposed to ratepayer GRT payment, which is within the purview of the Authority. To provide a residential GRT to a commercial establishment, Yankee allows nursing homes to receive residential tariff service. CNG and Southern stated that there is a spectrum between a hospital and a residence, which is a gray area and includes such entities as nursing homes, extended care facilities, and rehab facilities. Tr. 1/30/15, pp. 48 and 49; CNG and Southern Responses to Interrogatory No. 4.

The Authority considered having the utilities offer an alternative commercial tariff reflecting a residential GRT or classifying nursing homes and similar for-profit operations as residential customers. However, at this time, the Authority does not have sufficient information concerning the number of customers affected, annual sales and revenue, and bill impacts to make a determination on the service assignment to such commercial businesses. Therefore, the utilities are directed to include testimony and billing determinants for commercial customers providing residential-like services in their next rate case. At that time, detailed customer impact information will be available to allow the Authority to make an informed decision on this issue. In the meantime, all utilities shall continue their present practices until their next rate increase request is adjudicated.

CONCLUSION

All customers, including those exercising choice, are required to pay the true statutory GRT built into their service tariff. The EDCs and LDCs shall develop distribution rates in a rate application to include the appropriate GRT as Yankee presently does. Regarding the SUT, utility customers classified as residential are exempt from this tax while non-residential customers may qualify for the exemption under certain conditions. Finally, as to the service assignment and assessment of the GRT on commercial customers providing residential-like services such as nursing homes, the Authority requires additional detailed information before it can make a determination. Therefore, the Companies shall continue their present practices until their next rate increase when the Authority can review this issue fully.

Orders

For the following Orders, the Company shall submit one original of the required documentation to the Executive Secretary, 10 Franklin Square, New Britain, Connecticut 06051 and file an electronic version through the Authority’s website at www.ct.gov/pura. Submissions filed in compliance with the Authority’s Orders must be identified by all three of the following: Docket Number, Title and Order Number. Compliance with orders shall commence and continue as indicated in each specific Order or until the Company requests and the Authority approves that the Company’s compliance is no longer required after a certain date.

In their next rate increase application, EDCs and LDCs shall include the true statutory GRT in distribution rates.

In their next rate increase application, EDCs and LDCs shall provide a customer count, annual sales and revenue, and bill impacts for all commercial customers providing residential-like services by rate class.
